claims.claim: Home was said to have floated/levitated out of one window and in through the next.
claims.quote: Home was said to have levitated out of the third storey window of one room, and back in through the window of the adjoining room in front of three witnesses (Adare, Captain Wynne, and Lord Lindsay).

claims.claim: The window levitation took place in 1868.
claims.quote: Home met one of his future closest friends in 1867; the young Lord Adare (later the 4th Earl of Dunraven)... The following year, Home was said to have levitated out of the third storey window of one room

claims.claim: Three witnesses were present: Lord Adare, Captain Wynne and Lord Lindsay.
claims.quote: in front of three witnesses (Adare, Captain Wynne, and Lord Lindsay)

claims.claim: The three witnesses could not agree on what they saw.
claims.quote: However, John Sladek has pointed out that all three witnesses gave contradictory information about the levitation

claims.claim: The witnesses contradicted themselves, not just each other.
claims.quote: all three witnesses gave contradictory information about the levitation, even contradicting themselves about specific details

claims.claim: Adare said the height was 70 feet, Lindsay said 85, Home said 80.
claims.quote: The windows were 85 feet from the street (Lindsay); 70 feet (Lindsay); 80 feet (Home)

claims.claim: Adare said the third floor, then the first floor.
claims.quote: on the third floor (Adare); on the first floor (Adare)

claims.claim: Adare said it was dark; Lindsay said there was bright moonlight.
claims.quote: It was dark (Adare); there was a bright moonlight (Lindsay).

claims.claim: A few days before the levitation Home opened the same window and stood on the outside ledge in front of two witnesses.
claims.quote: A few days before the levitation, scaring Lord Lindsay, Home had opened the same window, stepped out and stood on the outside ledge in the presence of two witnesses.

claims.claim: McCabe noted the window-sill outside was nineteen inches wide.
claims.quote: he acknowledges that there was a nineteen-inch window-sill outside the window, and Home could stand on that

claims.claim: McCabe noted that no one claims to have seen Home travel between the windows.
claims.quote: No one professes to have seen Home carried from window to window.

claims.claim: William Crookes was a Fellow of the Royal Society (F.R.S.).
claims.quote: WILLIAM CROOKES, F. R. S. / Membre de la Société Royale de Londres [printed on crookestitlepage.jpg]

claims.claim: Crookes tested Home from 1870 to 1873 and published that the phenomena were genuine.
claims.quote: Between 1870 and 1873, chemist and physicist William Crookes conducted experiments to determine the validity of the phenomena produced by three mediums: Florence Cook, Kate Fox, and Home. Crookes' final report in 1874 concluded that the phenomena produced by all three mediums were genuine

claims.claim: The scientific establishment derided Crookes' conclusion.
claims.quote: a result which was roundly derided by the scientific establishment

claims.claim: Home's accordion played only two tunes, Home Sweet Home and The Last Rose of Summer, both within a single octave.
claims.quote: It was reported by sitters and Crookes that Home's accordion played only two pieces, Home Sweet Home and The Last Rose of Summer. Both contain only one-octave.

claims.claim: There was a four-foot gap between two iron balconies.
claims.quote: suggested rather than levitating Home had stepped across a gap of four feet between two iron balconies

claims.claim: Trevor H. Hall placed the levitation at Ashley Place, Westminster, at a height of 35 feet.
claims.quote: Trevor H. Hall who researched the case in detail established that the levitation took place at Ashley Place in Westminster at a height of 35 feet

claims.claim: Gordon Stein agreed the gap between the balconies was crossable on foot.
claims.quote: Gordon Stein also noted that the gap between the two balconies was only four feet making passing between them entirely feasible.

claims.claim: Home was privately caught faking hands and feet more than once, but never publicly exposed.
claims.where: card 6 note; caption paragraph 4 and final line
claims.quote: It is simply that Home was never publicly exposed in fraud. Privately, he was caught in fraud several times.

claims.claim: A sitter at Ealing in 1855 said the 'spirit hand' was a false limb attached to Home's arm.
claims.quote: At a séance in the house of the solicitor John Snaith Rymer in Ealing in July 1855, a sitter (Frederick Merrifield) observed that a "spirit-hand" was in fact a false limb attached on the end of Home's arm.

claims.claim: In Biarritz in 1857 a physician's letter described Home slipping off a thin shoe and using his foot to produce effects.
claims.quote: Count Perovsky-Petrovo-Solovovo described a letter by Dr. Barthez, a physician in the court of Empress Eugenie, which claimed a sitter Morio de l'lle caught Home using his foot to fake supposed spirit effects during a séance in Biarritz in 1857. Home wore thin shoes, easy to take off and draw on

claims.claim: The accordion cage experiment took place under a dining table and the amount of light was not stated.
claims.quote: However, the amount of light in the room was not stated, and the accordion was not observed in good light.

claims.claim: Podmore noted the accordion's keys were never observed to move.
claims.quote: According to Frank Podmore there was no evidence the accordion played at all, as the keys were not observed to have moved.

claims.claim: The window levitation is what made Home one of the most famous men of his era.
claims.quote: His biographer Peter Lamont opines that he was one of the most famous men of his era.

claims.claim: No explanation of the window incident has ever been proved.
claims.quote: Another possible natural explanation for Home's famous levitation was proposed by the psychical researcher Guy William Lambert

claims.quote: Archive title: File:Daniel Dunglas Home by Nadar.jpg ... Author: Nadar

claims.claim: The seated carte portrait is by the Atelier Nadar.
claims.quote: Author: Atelier Nadar. Photographe
